questions.q: Which resident connective tissue cell is derived from circulating blood monocytes and functions in phagocytosis and antigen presentation?
questions.explain: Tissue macrophages (histiocytes) differentiate from blood monocytes that migrate into connective tissue, where they phagocytose debris and present antigens to T lymphocytes.

open.q: Name the resident connective tissue phagocyte that differentiates from circulating blood monocytes.

questions.q: Which connective tissue cell contains numerous basophilic, metachromatic granules rich in histamine and heparin and mediates immediate hypersensitivity (type I anaphylactic) reactions?
questions.explain: Mast cells possess abundant cytoplasmic granules containing histamine, heparin, and neutral proteases that stain metachromatically with toluidine blue and degranulate upon IgE cross-linking.

open.q: Which tissue-resident immune cell releases histamine and heparin from metachromatic granules during IgE-mediated allergic reactions?

questions.q: Which distinctive nuclear chromatin arrangement characterizes antibody-secreting plasma cells on histological sections?
questions.explain: Plasma cells differentiate from activated B lymphocytes and feature abundant basophilic cytoplasm (rER), a pale paranuclear Golgi halo, and an eccentric round nucleus with alternating heterochromatin clumps arranged like spokes of a wheel or clock face.

open.q: Describe the characteristic appearance and position of the nucleus in an antibody-producing plasma cell.

questions.q: Which type of collagen is the most abundant in the human body, forming thick eosinophilic bundles in bone, tendons, ligaments, and the dermis?
questions.explain: Type I collagen accounts for roughly 90% of total body collagen, forming large, banded tensile fibers in skin, bone, tendons, ligaments, and organ capsules.

open.q: Which specific type of fibrillar collagen predominates in tendons, ligaments, dermis, and bone?

questions.q: Which collagen type forms fine, branching reticular fibers that create the supporting stroma of lymphoid organs, bone marrow, and liver sinusoids, and stains black with silver impregnation (argyrophilic)?
questions.explain: Reticular fibers consist of thin fibrils of type III collagen coated with glycoproteins and proteoglycans; they stain positively with PAS and black with silver stains (argyrophilic).

open.q: Which collagen type constitutes the argyrophilic reticular fibers supporting the stroma of lymph nodes, spleen, and bone marrow?

questions.q: A 19-year-old tall, thin man presents with lens dislocation (ectopia lentis), arachnodactyly, and ascending aortic aneurysm (Marfan syndrome). Mutation in which extracellular glycoprotein essential for elastic fiber assembly causes this disorder?
questions.explain: Marfan syndrome is caused by mutations in the FBN1 gene encoding fibrillin-1, which forms the microfibrillar scaffold upon which tropoelastin is deposited to construct elastic fibers.

open.q: Mutations in which microfibril-forming glycoprotein impair elastic fiber integrity in Marfan syndrome?

questions.q: Vitamin C (ascorbic acid) deficiency impairs collagen synthesis and causes scurvy because it is an essential cofactor for which post-translational enzymatic step?
options: Hydroxylation of proline and lysine residues in procollagen
Cleavage of C-terminal propeptides in the extracellular space
Cross-linking of tropocollagen by lysyl oxidase
Transcription of procollagen mRNA in the nucleus
questions.explain: Prolyl hydroxylase and lysyl hydroxylase require vitamin C as a cofactor to hydroxylate proline and lysine residues on procollagen alpha chains, enabling stable triple-helix hydrogen bonding.

open.q: Which post-translational modification of procollagen requires vitamin C as an essential cofactor and fails in scurvy?

questions.sub: Connective Tissue Proper and Adipose Tissue
questions.q: Which specialized connective tissue is found in the umbilical cord (Wharton jelly) and consists of stellate mesenchymal cells suspended in an abundant, hydrated hyaluronic acid-rich ground substance?
questions.explain: Mucoid connective tissue (Wharton jelly) is an embryonic connective tissue rich in hyaluronan with sparse collagen fibrils and stellate fibroblasts, cushioning the umbilical vessels.

open.q: What type of embryonic connective tissue constitutes Wharton jelly of the umbilical cord?

questions.sub: Connective Tissue Proper and Adipose Tissue
questions.q: Brown (multilocular) adipose tissue generates heat via non-shivering thermogenesis in neonates because its abundant mitochondria express which inner membrane protein?
questions.explain: Brown adipocytes contain numerous small lipid droplets and abundant mitochondria containing uncoupling protein-1 (thermogenin), which dissipates the proton gradient as heat instead of synthesizing ATP.

open.q: Name the inner mitochondrial membrane protein in brown adipose tissue that uncouples oxidative phosphorylation to generate heat.

questions.q: Which type of cartilage forms the articular surfaces of synovial joints, costal cartilages, tracheal rings, and the fetal skeleton model, and contains predominantly type II collagen?
questions.explain: Hyaline cartilage is the most common cartilage type, characterized by a glassy, basophilic territorial matrix rich in type II collagen fibrils and aggrecan proteoglycans; articular hyaline cartilage lacks a perichondrium.

open.q: Which type of cartilage covers the articular surfaces of synovial joints and forms the C-shaped rings of the trachea?

questions.q: Which type of cartilage lacks a perichondrium, contains dense bundles of type I collagen alongside type II collagen, and forms the intervertebral discs, pubic symphysis, and menisci?
questions.explain: Fibrocartilage is a transitional tissue combining features of dense regular connective tissue (thick type I collagen bundles) and hyaline cartilage (chondrocytes in rows within lacunae), always lacking a perichondrium.

open.q: Name the tough, perichondrium-free cartilage composed of alternating rows of chondrocytes and thick type I collagen bundles found in intervertebral discs.

questions.q: Which type of cartilage is found in the auricle (pinna) of the ear, external acoustic meatus, auditory tube, and epiglottis?
questions.explain: Elastic cartilage contains a dense network of branching elastic fibers in addition to type II collagen and is always surrounded by a vascular perichondrium, providing flexible shape retention in the pinna and epiglottis.

open.q: Which variety of cartilage provides flexible structural support to the epiglottis and external ear?

questions.q: Why does damaged hyaline cartilage heal slowly and poorly in adults?
options: Avascular cartilage depends on diffusion for nutrition and repair
questions.explain: Mature cartilage is completely avascular, alymphatic, and aneural; nutrients and oxygen must diffuse through the hydrated matrix from perichondrial vessels or synovial fluid, severely limiting repair.

open.q: What key vascular characteristic of mature cartilage accounts for its slow and limited capacity for repair after injury?

questions.q: Which multinucleated bone-resorbing cell is derived from granulocyte-macrophage progenitor cells (monocyte lineage) and sits within shallow depressions called Howship lacunae?
questions.explain: Osteoclasts are large, motile, multinucleated giant cells of hematopoietic monocyte-macrophage origin that polarize with a ruffled border and sealing zone to resorb mineralized bone matrix in Howship lacunae.

open.q: Name the large multinucleated bone-resorbing cell of monocyte-macrophage lineage that occupies Howship lacunae.

questions.q: Through which microscopic channels do cytoplasmic processes of osteocytes extend to communicate via gap junctions and receive nutrients across mineralized bone matrix?
questions.explain: Canaliculi are tiny radial channels penetrating the mineralized bone lamellae, linking adjacent osteocyte lacunae with each other and with the central Haversian canal.

open.q: Name the microscopic radial channels in bone matrix through which osteocyte processes exchange nutrients and signals via gap junctions.

questions.q: Which transverse or oblique vascular channels connect adjacent Haversian (central) canals with one another and with the periosteal and endosteal surfaces of compact bone?
questions.explain: Volkmann (perforating) canals run perpendicular or obliquely to the long axis of osteons without surrounding concentric lamellae, carrying blood vessels and nerves from the periosteum/endosteum into Haversian canals.

open.q: Name the transverse vascular channels in compact bone that lack concentric lamellae and connect Haversian canals to the periosteum and marrow cavity.

questions.q: What is the normal approximate diameter of a mature human erythrocyte (red blood cell) on a peripheral blood smear, often used as a 'histological ruler'?
questions.explain: A normal biconcave, anucleate erythrocyte measures approximately 7.5 micrometers in diameter and 2.6 micrometers at its rim, serving as a reliable internal size reference on tissue sections.

open.q: What is the approximate diameter in micrometers of a normal mature human red blood cell?

questions.q: Which granulocyte has a bilobed nucleus and large refractile eosinophilic specific granules containing major basic protein that are toxic to helminthic parasites?
questions.explain: Eosinophils constitute 1-4% of circulating leukocytes, feature a characteristic bilobed nucleus, and possess bright red-orange specific granules with crystalline cores of major basic protein.

open.q: Which polymorphonuclear leukocyte features a bilobed nucleus and bright red-orange cytoplasmic granules containing major basic protein?

questions.q: In females, an inactivated X chromosome may appear as a small drumstick-shaped nuclear appendage attached to one of the nuclear lobes of which leukocyte?
questions.explain: In approximately 2-3% of neutrophils in genetic females (46,XX), the condensed inactive X chromosome (Barr body) projects from a nuclear lobe as a tiny drumstick appendage.

open.q: In which circulating white blood cell does the Barr body appear as a tiny drumstick-shaped appendage extending from a nuclear lobe?

questions.q: From which giant polyploid bone marrow cell do circulating blood platelets (thrombocytes) bud off via demarcation membranes?
questions.explain: Megakaryocytes are huge polyploid (up to 64n) bone marrow cells that extend proplatelet processes through sinusoidal endothelium, shedding membrane-bound cytoplasmic fragments as platelets.

open.q: Name the giant polyploid bone marrow precursor cell that fragments its cytoplasm to produce blood platelets.
